sections.label: Extradition regime modernisation objective
sections.summary: The Bill's amendments aim to modernise Singapore's extradition regime and enhance international cooperation against crime.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: As such, the policy objective of the proposed amendments in the Bill is the modernisation of our extradition regime.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: This will enhance Singapore's credibility as a responsible international citizen to strengthen our ability to combat crime through international cooperation; ensure that Singapore is better able to facilitate extradition where justified; and secure the return of fugitives who have committed offences in Singapore.

sections.label: Two-year extraditable offence threshold
sections.summary: Clause 2 makes an offence extraditable if it carries a maximum punishment of two years' imprisonment or more, unless excluded.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Many other common law jurisdictions, such as Australia, Canada, Malaysia, New Zealand and the UK as well as jurisdictions in France, Germany, Japan and the Republic of Korea, have since adopted the threshold approach.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: So, in this case, under clause 2 of the Bill, section 2 now provides that an offence is extraditable as long as it has a maximum punishment of two years' imprisonment or more and is not on the list of excluded offences.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: The threshold of a maximum punishment of two years' imprisonment or more is commonly adopted internationally.

sections.label: Extraditable offence punishment threshold
sections.summary: An offence with a maximum punishment of two years' imprisonment or more is extraditable unless it is on the excluded offences list.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: If it attracts a maximum punishment of two years' imprisonment, or more, it is extraditable as long as it is not on the list of excluded offences.

sections.label: Clause 6 new restrictions
sections.summary: Clause 6 of the Bill inserts four new restrictions under new sections 8 and 9.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Clause 6 of the Bill inserts four new restrictions under new sections 8 and 9.

sections.label: Rejecting request for short remaining term
sections.summary: Singapore may reject a request if the fugitive's remaining imprisonment term to serve is less than six months.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Singapore may reject the request if the remaining imprisonment term which the fugitive has to serve is less than six months.

sections.label: Fugitive consent to surrender
sections.summary: The amendments allow a fugitive to indicate to the Magistrate consent to surrender at any time after arrest.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: The amendments, therefore, allow a fugitive to indicate to the Magistrate that he or she wishes to consent to his or her surrender at any time after the arrest.

sections.label: Review of Magistrate release decisions
sections.summary: The Act does not let the Attorney-General seek review of a Magistrate's release decision, so new section 17 consolidates review procedures and adds this mechanism.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: However, the Act does not, at present, provide for the Attorney-General, on behalf of the requesting state, to similarly apply for a review of a Magistrate's decision to release the fugitive.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: We have, therefore, consolidated the applicable procedures for a review of a Magistrate's order in the new section 17.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Second, it introduces a new mechanism to allow the Attorney-General, on behalf of the requesting state, to apply to the High Court to review a Magistrate's decision to release the fugitive.

sections.label: Record of the case mechanism
sections.summary: Clause 15 introduces a record of the case mechanism under new section 44 to simplify admitting evidence justifying a fugitive's extradition.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Clause 15 of the Bill introduces a record of the case mechanism under a new section 44, which will simplify the procedure for admission of evidence to justify the extradition of a fugitive.

sections.label: New Fourth Schedule extradition offences
sections.summary: Clause 18 inserts a new Fourth Schedule listing extradition offences from Singapore's international obligations currently found in other statutes.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Clause 18 of the Bill inserts a new Fourth Schedule to the Act which lists the extradition offences arising from Singapore's international obligations that are currently found in other statutes.

sections.label: Consolidated extradition framework
sections.summary: The Bill consolidates the extradition framework for foreign states and declared Commonwealth territories into a single framework.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: The Bill consolidates the extradition framework for foreign states and declared Commonwealth territories into a single framework.

sections.label: New Parts 3 and 4
sections.summary: The Bill creates new Part 3 for extradition from Singapore and Part 4 for extradition to Singapore, while preserving the Malaysia Part.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: The Bill provides for a new Part 3 for “Extradition From Singapore” and a new Part 4 for “Extradition To Singapore”, so, simplifying it into two buckets – to Singapore or from Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: For completeness, Sir, I should add that, aside from minor updating of the language, we have preserved the Part on “Extradition To and From Malaysia”, by way of endorsements of arrest warrants.

sections.label: Purpose of the extradition Bill
sections.summary: The Bill updates and modernises Singapore's domestic extradition regime, ensures state and judicial resources are not over-used, and cements Singapore's role as a responsible global citizen.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: With these amendments, Singapore will enhance its ability to combat crime through international cooperation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: As outlined by the Minister, the purpose of the Bill is to update and modernise our domestic extradition regime; ensure that there are mechanisms to ensure that resources of the state and judicial system are not over-used; and cement Singapore’s role as a responsible global citizen.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: As a result, this Bill proposes to make what I believe to be the most substantial amendments to the Act since it was enacted 54 years ago.

sections.label: Foreign States treaty definition
sections.summary: Ms Brabyn listed 14 more states potentially meeting the Foreign States definition from 1898-1960 UK treaties; the speaker says 54 years was enough time to identify enforceable treaties.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: In her article, Ms Brabyn listed 14 more states that can potentially fulfil the definition of “Foreign States” arising from treaties entered into between 1898 and 1960 with the UK.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: In my respectful view, the passage of 54 years since the enactment of the Act constitutes more than enough time for the Government to have ascertained which are the historical treaties that Singapore considers as bilaterally enforceable.

sections.label: Minister cancelling court warrants
sections.summary: The speaker is concerned about giving the Minister power to cancel a warrant issued by the Court, an independent pillar of Government.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Having regard to the separation of powers in our Westminster-style Government, I am concerned about arrogating to the Minister a power to cancel a warrant issued by the Court, which is an independent pillar of our Government.

sections.label: Attorney-General invoking extradition powers
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether only the Attorney-General or his appointee should invoke the Act's extradition powers, as in MACMA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Would it not be better to explicitly ensure that no other party other than the Attorney-General or someone appointed by him may invoke the powers of the Act to extradite a fugitive, just like in MACMA?

sections.label: Reconciling treaties listing offences
sections.summary: The speaker asks how this approach can be reconciled with treaties that list offences, rather than adopting the threshold approach.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: My question is: how are we able to reconcile this approach with respect to treaties which list offences, as opposed to adopting the threshold approach?

sections.label: Brunei extradition arrangement omission
sections.summary: The Bill is silent on the extradition arrangement with Brunei.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The Bill is, however, silent on the extradition arrangement with Brunei.

sections.label: Court discretion over public interest
sections.summary: The speaker notes MACMA section 22(4)(c) requires a Court to be satisfied a production order is not contrary to Singapore's public interest, and says the Court should have similar judicial discretion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: In this regard, I wish to point out that under section 22(4)(c) of MACMA, it is specifically provided that a Court, before it issues a production order for the benefit of foreign criminal proceedings, should satisfy itself that the issuance of the production order is not contrary to Singapore’s public interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: I am also aware that under the proposed section 10(2)(d) in the Bill, there is a discretion provided to the Minister not to order a fugitive to be arrested for “any other sufficient cause”.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Even if it does, my main point is that the Court should be given the judicial discretion to consider Singapore’s public interest, just like in the case for MACMA.

sections.label: Magistrate discretion in extradition
sections.summary: The speaker argued a magistrate should have more discretion to apply Singapore's public interest in extradition decisions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: On the other hand, for a magistrate deciding whether or not to order extradition, I argued the reverse: that he should be given more discretion to apply Singapore's public interest.

sections.label: Extraditable offence threshold
sections.summary: Once the Bill is effective, the threshold for an extraditable offence will be offences attracting a maximum imprisonment of two years or more, subject to exclusions.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Once the Bill is effective, the threshold for an extraditable offence will be simply set at offences attracting a maximum imprisonment of two years or more, subject to the list of exclusions.

sections.label: Protections and time-barred prohibition
sections.summary: The Bill re-enacts and expands protections to all treaty countries and prohibits extradition if the alleged offence is time-barred under the foreign state's law.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: These protections are re-enacted and expanded in the Bill to apply to all treaty countries.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: There will also now be a specific prohibition in the proposed section 8 against the extradition of a person if his alleged offence is time-barred based on the law of the foreign state – a point which the Minister touched on earlier.

sections.label: Indonesia extradition treaty history
sections.summary: A prior bilateral extradition treaty signed around 2007 was not implemented due to hurdles in Indonesia's domestic approval process, and the new treaty allows retrospective application.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: A prior bilateral extradition treaty was signed around 2007, but it was not implemented due to hurdles in the domestic approval process in Indonesia.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In February this year, Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean told the House that the new extradition treaty contained a provision to allow for retrospective application to extradite fugitives for crimes committed 18 years ago.

sections.label: Indonesia treaty and Roach extradition
sections.summary: The Minister was asked whether the Bill affects arrangements under the Indonesia treaty, and the Roach case involved an assurance against caning and remission of the sentence.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Earlier, the Minister mentioned in the Second Reading speech that when this year's bilateral treaty with Indonesia is in force, Indonesia and Singapore can extradite fugitives based on the terms of that treaty.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Can the Minister confirm whether this Bill will affect those arrangements and, if so, how?

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In the case of Mr Roach mentioned earlier, the Singapore Government has secured his extradition from the UK after giving an assurance to the UK government that he would not undergo the punishment of caning.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: After Mr Roach was duly convicted of robbery in Singapore and sentenced to the mandatory six strokes of the cane, the Government advised the President to exercise her constitutional powers to remit the sentence of caning so as to honour its assurance to the UK government.

sections.label: Surrender to Commonwealth territories
sections.summary: The Minister was asked to clarify why the surrender of persons to Commonwealth territories is restricted in special ways.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Can the Minister clarify why the surrender of persons to Commonwealth territories is restricted in special ways?

sections.label: Minister discretion in cases
sections.summary: The passage asks the Minister to share scenarios on how discretion is meant to be exercised for such cases.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Can the Minister share scenarios on how discretion is meant to be exercised for such cases?

sections.label: Extradition evidence and Minister powers
sections.summary: The Bill lets a requesting foreign jurisdiction provide evidence by summarising it, and section 10 restricts the Minister's surrender powers on persecution grounds.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The Bill allows a foreign jurisdiction requesting extradition to provide evidence by, in essence, summarising it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: For instance, section 10 restricts the Minister's powers to order the surrender of persons if the Minister has substantial grounds for believing that the person would be persecuted for reasons of race, religion, sex, ethnic origin, nationality or political opinion.

sections.label: New extraditable offence threshold
sections.summary: Under the amendment Bill, an offence is extraditable under the threshold approach if it attracts two or more years' imprisonment, subject to excluded offences.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: Instead of having to come within specific offences in a list under the existing approach, an offence will now be extraditable under the new threshold approach in this amendment Bill if it attracts a punishment of two or more years of imprisonment, subject to the list of excluded offences.

sections.label: Prohibition and SAF Act offences
sections.summary: The passage asks whether the prohibition applies as long as the fugitive is charged for actions constituting an offence under the SAF Act and subsidiary legislation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: Do I understand correctly that the prohibition will apply as long as the fugitive is charged for actions which, if it had happened in Singapore, would constitute an offence under our Singapore Armed Forces Act (SAF Act) and any subsidiary legislation?

sections.label: Consent and Magistrate examination
sections.summary: The passage seeks clarification whether a fugitive's consent obviates the Magistrate's need to examine that the proposed extradition prima facie meets the Extradition Act's requirements.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: I agree that this may save state resources in otherwise having to proceed with a more lengthy extradition proceeding.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: However, I would like to seek clarification from the Minister whether a consent by a fugitive will obviate the need for the Magistrate hearing the case to still examine and ensure that, prima facie, the proposed extradition comes within the requirements of the Extradition Act, regardless of and independent of the reasons or circumstances for him or her choosing to consent.

sections.label: Safeguards against record abuses
sections.summary: The passage asks what safeguards exist against abuses such as inaccuracies or inadequacies in the record of the case.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: While it is supposed to simplify and, while I note that the Bill does provide for the Court retaining discretion in determining the weight to be given to the evidence admitted by way of the record of the case, I would like to ask what are the safeguards against abuses, for example, where there are inaccuracies, deliberate or otherwise, or any inadequacies with regard to the record of the case.

sections.label: Pre-Independence Extradition Treaties Applying
sections.summary: Only the 1872 Germany and 1935 US pre-Independence treaties apply to Singapore; other UK pre-Independence extradition treaties do not.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The short answer, therefore, to Mr Murali Pillai's question is that only our pre-Independence treaties with Germany, entered into in 1872, and the US, entered into in 1935, apply to Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: None of the other pre-Independence extradition treaties entered into by the UK currently applies to Singapore.

sections.label: Political Character Restriction Exception
sections.summary: The political character restriction does not apply to offences against the life or person of a political figure and immediate family in declared Commonwealth territories.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In other words, the "political character" restriction does not apply in respect of an offence against the life or person of a political figure and his or her immediate family for declared Commonwealth territories.

sections.label: Saving Provisions for Existing Treaties
sections.summary: Saving provisions in the Bill preserve the status quo in existing extradition treaties, so amendments generally would not apply to them.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Saving provisions have been drafted in the Bill to preserve the status quo in our existing extradition treaties, which means that amendments would, generally, not apply to our extradition treaties.

sections.label: US Bilateral Treaty Offence Categories
sections.summary: The US could not rely on the bilateral treaty to request extradition for an offence outside the treaty's offence categories.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The US would not be able to rely on the bilateral treaty to request extradition of a fugitive wanted for an offence that is not within the categories of offences in the treaty.

sections.label: Alternative Evidence and Committal Standard
sections.summary: A prosecutor may summarise arrest circumstances instead of many affidavits, but the prima facie evidence standard for committal is not lowered.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: For example, it may suffice for a prosecutor of the requesting state to summarise the circumstances of the fugitive's arrest, rather than to include numerous affidavits from each witness and every arresting officer to describe their individual roles and capacities in which the fugitive was apprehended.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: It provides an alternative means to presenting evidence but does not in any way mean that the bar or the standard of evidence that has to be reached for the threshold for assessment of committal for this fugitive is to be lowered.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: There must still be sufficient evidence to prove a prima facie case, in other words, on the face of it, that there is sufficient corroborating evidence that the fugitive, indeed, committed such an offence.

sections.label: Magistrate Committal and Release Powers
sections.summary: A Magistrate may commit a fugitive only with sufficient evidence justifying extradition, and must release the fugitive in all other circumstances.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Under the Act, a Magistrate is only entitled to commit the fugitive to prison if the Magistrate is satisfied that there is sufficient evidence to justify his or her extradition; or the Magistrate has to release the fugitive in all other circumstances.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In other words, as long as there is a prima facie case that would justify the trial of the fugitive, or sufficient evidence that the fugitive had been convicted of that offence, the Magistrate must order the committal of the fugitive.

sections.label: Extradition court applications by AGC
sections.summary: Extradition requests are made government-to-government, and Court applications under the Extradition Act would be made by Attorney-General's Chambers officers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Since extradition requests are made solely at the government-to-government level, as Mr Murali Pillai alluded to, Court applications under the Extradition Act would be made by officers from the Attorney-General's Chambers.

sections.label: Expected extradition caseload after amendments
sections.summary: The speaker says section 16 release is dealt with and no extraordinary spike in caseload is expected from the amendments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: I think I have dealt with section 16 as to when the Magistrate will order the release.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: We do not expect there to be an unusual or heavy spike.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: But, of course, with the provisions here, we will have to look at what the caseload might turn out to be.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: I do not think this will be something that is extraordinary or anomalous, but, as I mentioned in my opening speech, our experience has been that states will continue to seek extradition for the most serious of offences, cases in which there is a significance, for which the fugitive is to be apprehended for serious offences.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: So, on that basis, we do not expect there to be an extraordinary spike given these amendments.

sections.label: Treaty 18-year period with Indonesia
sections.summary: The treaty's agreed period with Indonesia goes back 18 years, and the treaty's terms govern extradition between the two states.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: So, is he saying that the Indonesians are now happy with just going back 18 years and they will just sort out whatever they need to do?

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: I think 18 years is the agreed period of time with Indonesia in the treaty.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: As to how and to what end they want to use that and deal with fugitives arising from the AFC or otherwise, I think that is a call that they make.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: But on the terms of the treaty, it goes back 18 years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: To the Member's first point, the treaty contains the substantive obligations between the two states.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: I think I pointed out both in my opening speech as well as my reply to the Member that that is the principle – you look at the treaty and the terms of the treaty and that governs the relationship between the two parties as to the terms on which you extradite or not extradite, as the case might be.
